title: Federal judge blocks Pentagon's Anthropic blacklist as First Amendment retaliation
subtitle: In a 59-page order, U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found the Defense Department's supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic was 'illegal and baseless' and violated the company's constitutional rights.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: U.S. District Judge Rita Lin issued a 59-page written order Thursday night blocking the Department of Defense from labeling Anthropic a supply-chain risk. Lin — a Biden appointee sitting in the Northern District of California — ruled that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's designation was 'illegal and baseless' and constituted 'unlawful retaliation' against the Claude maker for its constitutionally protected speech. The order also cites a due-process violation under the Fifth Amendment. The dispute began in February when the Trump administration accused Anthropic of endangering national security after the company refused to allow military use of Claude for U.S. surveillance or autonomous weapons. The Pentagon is expected to appeal.

The mechanism matters as much as the outcome. Lin's order says the government cannot use national-security authorities to punish a vendor for publicly criticizing administration policy — the risk-designation statute does not permit sweeping penalties based 'principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views.' That reasoning gives AI developers a concrete legal shield when they draw usage limits the government dislikes, rather than being forced to choose between their safety policies and access to federal contracts.

It is the first substantive court win in an eighteen-month arc of AI-vendor-vs-government disputes. The same court granted Anthropic a temporary block in March; this week's ruling converts that pause into a merits finding on First Amendment grounds. Read alongside the FTC's 2025 open inquiry into frontier-model contracts and Europe's AI Act transparency rules that took effect August 2, it fits a pattern: courts and regulators are beginning to write in the boundary between what a government can compel a frontier lab to do and what a lab is allowed to refuse.

Takeaway for learners: 'refusal capabilities' aren't just a model-behavior topic. When a vendor writes 'no autonomous weapons' or 'no mass surveillance' into a usage policy, that clause is now — at least in one circuit — protected speech. If you work on trust-and-safety, procurement, or policy at any AI-adjacent organization, read the actual usage policies of the models you deploy; those documents just gained legal weight.
